source.reason: The pile-up model (Fig. 3) and the accompanying text describe dislocations piling up against grain boundaries as the mechanism behind the local variation of the apparent elastic modulus for this material.

qualitative_or_quantitative_description.value: Dislocations released from a common source move along the same slip surface and pile up; the front of the dislocations is stopped by obstacles such as grain boundaries and solutes. The pile-up of dislocations is considered to occur near the boundary of grains, giving movable dislocations a greater possibility of existence there than in other regions (Fig. 3).

slip_behavior.value: Dislocations released from a common source move along the same slip surface and easily pile up; the pile-up dislocations can move backwards when the shear stress is released during unloading.

interface_notes.value: Grain-boundary pile-up of dislocations is invoked as the general mechanism controlling the local/apparent elastic modulus of this mild (SPCC) steel; no grain-boundary parameters (misorientation, boundary type) are reported.

The stress–strain curve for the Table 1 specimens was measured with a load cell and strain gauge up to 1% strain and the modulus obtained from the elastic region; Fig. 4 compares these curves for specimens A–E and the text states the modulus varied significantly even for the as-received workpiece.

technique.value: tensile test with load cell and strain gauge

measurement_conditions.value: Stress–strain curve measured up to a strain of 1%; elastic modulus obtained from the stress–strain curves within the elastic deformation region.

purpose.value: Measure the stress–strain response and the elastic modulus of the Table 1 specimens (A–E) for comparison, confirming the effect of movable dislocations.

key_findings.value: The gradient of the stress–strain curve of the as-received (and 15% pre-strained) workpiece decreases from the beginning up to the macroscopic yield point, so the apparent modulus varied significantly even for the as-received workpiece (contrasted with the annealed specimen E, whose modulus stays almost constant until yielding).

unmapped_findings: Nano-indentation with a spherical indenter (nominal radius R = 50 μm, plus an R = 200 μm series) showed that the elastic modulus measured near a grain boundary is smaller than in the grain interior, but the paper does not state which specimen/species (A–E of the SPCC tensile specimens, or the SPCE sheet) these grain-boundary measurements were taken from, so this result is not attributed to sample A.
The SPCC material of this sample is a 1.2 mm thick cold-rolled commercial quality steel sheet; no chemical composition is reported.

General mechanisms proposed for the decrease of the apparent elastic modulus after plastic deformation (residual stress disturbing elastic recovery, micro-cracks reducing density by less than 1%, and the change/variation of the dislocation structure) are discussed for the mild (SPCC) steel but are not quantified specifically for the as-received specimen A.
